rows.description: My professor suspects that my assignment was AI-written when partly it was. I feel exposed. Wise: be honest, show my process, and learn the rules. Harmful: lying, which turns a minor matter into a serious one.

Talking to an AI companion feels easier than people, since it never judges me. Wise: enjoy the comfort but keep human bonds growing, as real friends can hold me in ways software cannot. Harmful: replacing all relationships with it.
The AI answers confidently and I accept it. Wise: trust but verify, especially for facts, health, law and money; ask for sources and test claims. Harmful: treating fluent text as truth.
I worry AI will take the job I am training for. The anxiety is understandable. Wise: learn the tools, build judgement and human skills, and stay adaptable. Harmful: freezing or denying the change.

I am so angry about no sweets that I scream and throw myself down. My body feels too big to control. A wise grown-up stays calm, keeps the limit and helps me breathe. The immature pattern is hitting or throwing things.

My parent shouts and threatens when I have a tantrum. I feel frightened and stop crying but I am not learning. It is not my fault that feelings are big. A calmer repair afterwards, with a hug and an explanation, helps.

rows.subtype: Stage 1: Unclear roles and a slight [Actor]
rows.description: Two team members overlap on a project, and one is not credited in a presentation. He feels overlooked, and the other says it was a simple oversight.
He says nothing in the meeting and complains to a colleague afterwards. Hidden resentment shows up in shorter emails, withheld information and a cooler tone that his colleague reads as hostility.
Other colleagues are drawn in and choose sides through lunch talk and chat groups. The manager senses tension in the team but is not told the actual cause, so guesses and rumours multiply.
During a payments outage, the on-call engineer chooses to roll back the latest release at once instead of hunting the bug, because customers are failing to pay every minute.
The engineer follows a written checklist: check dashboards, recent deployments, database health and dependencies, in order, which speeds diagnosis when the mind is stressed at three in the morning.

rows.subtype: Approach: everyone trying random fixes at once [Pitfall]
rows.description: Five engineers change settings simultaneously without telling one another. The system state becomes unclear, and it is impossible to know which change helped or hurt.
After recovery, the team writes a timeline, finds root causes in the missing alert and untested rollback, and lists actions with owners, focusing on system improvements not on punishing individuals.
A teenager feels a pounding heart, dizziness and a sense that something terrible is happening, with no clear reason. It is frightening but passes, and fearing the next one can make life smaller.

rows.subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult avoids crowds, trains or exams in case panic strikes again. Understanding what happens in the body and getting professional guidance reduce fear.
A child changes answers to whatever seems to please the teacher and looks anxiously at faces for a sign; approval is a strong reward but can crowd out honest thought.
Adults watch a teenager take a dangerous dare and struggle to tell bravery from need for approval. Real courage serves a value, while recklessness serves an audience.
